title: 1:1 Should Mean Access, Not Screen Time
author: Marcinek, Andrew
summary: Marcinek argues that schools launching 1:1 device programs almost universally send home a logistics letter and skip the one question families actually want answered: why does my child have this device at all? He engages seriously with the current backlash against school devices, including Jared Cooney Horvath's The Digital Delusion, conceding its fair points while rejecting its conflation of a teacher-assigned Chromebook with a student's personal phone. His fix is 'default off': devices stay closed by default and open only when a teacher names a specific instructional purpose, a discipline best enforced by pre-planning exactly when lids go up and down before the lesson starts. He backs this with OECD findings that purposeful, moderate device use correlates with stronger performance while heavy or leisure use correlates with weaker performance, and cites synthesis research showing 1:1 programs help only when paired with real teacher planning time. The piece includes a full model letter reframing parent communication around a stated philosophy of learning rather than only insurance and rules.
points: Most 1:1 program letters cover insurance and acceptable-use policy but never explain to families why the device exists in the first place.
'Default off' is not an anti-technology stance — done right it should sometimes conclude the right tool is paper, discussion, or a lab bench instead.
OECD data shows purposeful, moderate device use tracks with stronger performance while heavy or leisure use tracks with weaker — outright bans don't move the needle either way.
The best synthesis research on 1:1 programs found real gains only where paired with planning support — a laptop by itself helps with nothing.
A model welcome letter should lead with the school's instructional philosophy for the device, asking a caregiver and student to sign a shared commitment rather than just a compliance form.
quotes: What families never hear is the one thing they actually want to know. Why is this device here in the first place?

It also does what most of the current backlash does: it treats the phone in a student's pocket and the Chromebook a teacher assigns as the same problem, and it draws sweeping conclusions from a base that is thinner than the movement behind it suggests.
A 1:1 program should guarantee every student access to a device when the learning calls for one. It should never mean every student has that device open all day.

It is also the pattern the OECD keeps finding when it looks at the data: moderate, purposeful device use for learning tracks with stronger performance, and heavy use or leisure use at school tracks with weaker.

The difference was never the hardware. It was whether anyone had decided what the device was for and given teachers the time to plan around it... its lead author was blunt that a laptop on its own helps with nothing.
For years our acceptable use agreements have told students everything they promise us... What if schools made some promises too? We will not put you on a device simply because we bought one.
One-to-one should mean one device available to every student. It should never mean one device open in front of every student. Default off. Open with purpose. Close when the purpose is gone.
